sections.title: What are Sorting Algorithms?
sections.content:
Sorting transforms chaos into order, and order enables faster algorithms. Binary search only works on sorted arrays. Two pointer techniques often require sorted input. Many greedy algorithms sort first then make locally optimal choices. Sorting is not just a prerequisite topic - it teaches core algorithmic techniques that appear repeatedly.

Each major sorting algorithm embodies a different technique. Merge sort teaches divide and conquer: split the problem in half, solve each half, merge the results. Quicksort teaches partitioning: pick a pivot, rearrange elements around it in O(n), then recurse on each side. Counting sort teaches the power of constraints: when you know elements are bounded integers, you can sort without any comparisons at all.

There is a fundamental lower bound for comparison-based sorting: any algorithm that sorts solely by comparing elements needs at least O(n log n) comparisons. This is a mathematical fact. There are n! possible orderings of n elements, and each comparison can eliminate at most half of them. Since log2(n!) is approximately n log n by Stirling's approximation, you need at least n log n comparisons. Merge sort and heapsort achieve this bound.

In interviews you are rarely asked to implement a sorting algorithm from scratch - but you are expected to know their trade-offs, when to use each one, and how their internal techniques (merge, partition) apply to other problems. Count inversions uses merge sort's merge step. Dutch National Flag (the quicksort partition) solves Sort Colors directly.

JavaScript has one notorious gotcha: `Array.sort()` sorts lexicographically by default. `[10, 9, 2].sort()` returns `[10, 2, 9]`. Always pass a numeric comparator: `.sort((a, b) => a - b)`. This mistake causes silent wrong answers on almost every sorting problem.

sections.title: When to Use This
sections.content: Reach for sorting when input needs to be ordered before applying another algorithm (binary search, two pointers, greedy), when stability matters (preserve relative order of equal elements - merge sort guarantees this, quicksort does not), or when you need to sort by a custom key or multiple criteria. Merge sort's merge step applies directly to problems involving two sorted arrays. The quicksort partition (Dutch National Flag) applies when you need to rearrange elements around a pivot value in O(n). Counting/radix sort applies when elements are non-negative integers in a small known range and O(n log n) is not fast enough.

sections.title: Merge Sort, Quicksort, and Counting Sort
sections.content:
## Merge Sort

**Divide** the array in half. **Sort** each half recursively. **Merge** the two sorted halves into one sorted array.

The merge step is the key technique: use two pointers, one on each sorted half. Repeatedly pick the smaller element and advance that pointer. This is O(n) per level, and there are O(log n) levels of recursion, giving O(n log n) total.

- Time: O(n log n) always (best, average, worst - no bad inputs)
- Space: O(n) extra for the temporary arrays during merge
- Stable: yes (equal elements from the left half come before right half)
- External sorting: merge sort is used when data does not fit in memory

## Quicksort

**Pick a pivot.** **Partition** the array: rearrange elements so everything smaller than the pivot is left of it and everything larger is right of it. **Recurse** on the left part and right part.

The partition step is O(n). With a good pivot (close to median), each partition splits the array roughly in half: O(log n) levels, O(n log n) total. With a bad pivot (always smallest or largest), partitions are lopsided: O(n) levels, O(n^2) total. An already-sorted array with `pivot = arr[0]` always produces the worst case.

- Time: O(n log n) average, O(n^2) worst case
- Space: O(log n) call stack (in-place, no extra array needed)
- Stable: **no** (partitioning can change relative order of equal elements)
- In practice: faster than merge sort on random data due to cache performance

## Dutch National Flag (3-way Partition)

A variant of the quicksort partition that handles three categories (less than, equal to, greater than pivot) in one O(n) pass. Uses three pointers: `low`, `mid`, `high`. Swap elements to their correct region as `mid` advances. This directly solves "Sort Colors" (sort 0s, 1s, 2s in one pass).

## Counting Sort and Radix Sort

When elements are **non-negative integers in a known range `[0, k]`**, you can sort in O(n + k) without any comparisons.

**Counting sort**: count how many times each value appears, then use prefix sums to find where each value belongs in the output. O(n + k) time and space. Only works for non-negative integers; k must be small relative to n.

**Radix sort**: sort digit by digit (least significant to most significant), using a stable counting sort at each digit level. Handles larger integers by reducing k to 10 (digits 0-9). O(d(n + k)) where d is number of digits.

## JavaScript `.sort()` Gotcha

JavaScript's built-in sort is **lexicographic by default**. Numbers are converted to strings and compared character by character. `[10, 9, 2].sort()` gives `[10, 2, 9]` because '1' < '2' < '9'. **Always** pass a comparator for numbers: `.sort((a, b) => a - b)` for ascending, `.sort((a, b) => b - a)` for descending.

sections.title: Core Template
sections.explanation: Merge sort is the cleanest to implement correctly and is most commonly asked in interviews. The partition function from quicksort is standalone-useful for Dutch National Flag problems. Both are shown here as the two most important templates to know.

items.name: Timsort (JS/Python Built-in)
items.description: The sorting algorithm used by JavaScript's `Array.sort()` and Python's `list.sort()`. A hybrid of merge sort and insertion sort that exploits naturally occurring sorted runs in the input. Stable, O(n log n) worst case. You do not implement it, but knowing it exists explains why built-in sort is faster in practice than a naive merge sort.

items.name: 3-Way Quicksort (Equal Elements)
items.description: Standard quicksort degrades to O(n^2) on inputs with many equal elements. 3-way quicksort partitions into three regions: less than, equal to, greater than. Elements equal to the pivot are already in final position and not recursed on. Best case becomes O(n) when all elements are equal.

items.name: Bucket Sort
items.description: Distribute elements into a number of buckets based on value range, sort each bucket (often with insertion sort), then concatenate. O(n + k) average when elements are uniformly distributed. Useful when input is floating point in a known range and distribution is roughly uniform.
items.example_problem: Kth Largest Element in an Array

sections.title: Complexity
sections.time: Merge sort: O(n log n) always. Quicksort: O(n log n) average, O(n^2) worst. Counting sort: O(n + k).
sections.space: Merge sort: O(n) extra. Quicksort: O(log n) stack. Counting sort: O(k).
sections.explanation: The O(n log n) lower bound for comparison sorts comes from the fact that there are n! permutations and each comparison eliminates at most half of them. Merge sort achieves this with O(n) extra space for merging. Quicksort achieves it on average with O(log n) stack space, but degrades to O(n^2) with bad pivot choices. Counting sort breaks the lower bound by not using comparisons - it uses the actual integer values as array indices.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Using JS `.sort()` without a comparator: numbers are sorted lexicographically by default. `[10,9,2].sort()` returns `[10,2,9]`. This is a silent bug - no error, just wrong order. Always pass `(a,b) => a-b`.
Assuming merge sort is in-place: merge sort requires O(n) extra space for the temporary merged arrays. If an interviewer says 'sort in O(1) space', merge sort is off the table.

Quicksort worst case on sorted input: if the pivot is always the first element and the input is already sorted, every partition produces a 0/n-1 split, degrading to O(n^2). Use random pivot or median-of-three to avoid this.
Treating quicksort as stable: quicksort reorders equal elements during partitioning. If the problem requires preserving the relative order of equal elements (stable sort), use merge sort instead.

Using counting sort for negative integers or unbounded ranges: counting sort requires non-negative integers and an array of size k. Negative values require offset adjustments; large k wastes O(k) space even if n is small.

items.title: Sort Colors
items.why: Directly applies the Dutch National Flag (3-way partition) technique from quicksort. Solve in one pass, O(n) time, O(1) space - reinforces that the partition step is useful beyond quicksort itself.

items.title: Merge Intervals
items.why: Sort intervals by start time first, then merge overlapping ones with a linear scan. Reinforces that sorting is often the first step that enables a simpler algorithm.

items.title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
items.why: Optimal solution is Quickselect: run one partition step, then recurse only on the side containing k. O(n) average. Directly uses the partition concept from quicksort without sorting the whole array.

items.title: Sort List
items.why: Merge sort on a linked list. Cannot use index-based access, so this forces implementation of the merge step on nodes. Tests whether you understand merge sort's structure independently of arrays.

sections.title: What to Learn Next
sections.why: Binary search requires sorted input to work. Having just learned how sorting works and why sorted order matters, binary search is the natural next step: it exploits the sorted property to find elements in O(log n) instead of O(n).
